Calibrate forecast distributions on recent years

Source: R/model-calibrate.R
calibrated.Rd

Wraps any model specification so that the spread (and optionally the trend) of its forecast draws is recalibrated on the last years observed years of the training data. Each time the model is fitted (also at every origin of an outer mt_backtest()):

Usage

calibrated(
  spec,
  years = 10,
  n_origins = 5,
  scale = c("horizon", "constant"),
  bias = FALSE,
  target = c("crps", "interval"),
  level = 0.95,
  by = NULL,
  n_draws = 100,
  seed = 1
)

Arguments

spec

A model specification.

years

Length of the calibration window (the last observed years).

n_origins

Number of origins in the window (evenly spaced from years to 2 years before the end of the training data).

scale

"horizon" (spread factor \(s_1 h^{\gamma}\)) or "constant".

bias

Estimate a correction of the drift (log rate per year).

target

"crps" or "interval" (interval score at level).

level

Level of the central interval for target = "interval".

by

Stratum variables with separate calibration parameters.

n_draws

Draws per inner forecast.

seed

Random seed of the inner forecasts and of the simulated observation noise.

Value

A model specification. The fitted object has a calibration element: a data.table with one row per group (scale_h1, slope, drift, the number of scored cells, and CRPS and coverage of the inner forecasts before and after calibration).

Details

  1. the base model is refitted at n_origins origins inside the calibration window (training data up to the origin) and forecasts the remaining years of the window;

  2. the draws are transformed per cell on the log scale, $$\log m^* = \tilde m + b\,h + s(h)\,(\log m - \tilde m),$$ where \(\tilde m\) is the median of the draws in the cell, \(h\) the horizon, \(s(h) = s_1 h^{\gamma}\) a spread factor (scale = "horizon"; \(\gamma = 0\) for scale = "constant"), constant beyond the longest horizon of the window, and \(b\) a correction of the drift per year (bias = TRUE);

  3. \(s_1\), \(\gamma\) and \(b\) minimise the mean CRPS (or the interval score, target) of the log death rates in the window, with Poisson (and the model's extra-Poisson) variation of the observed deaths, as in mt_backtest(). Draws of an ensemble get the observation noise of the component they come from.

The final model is fitted on all training data and its forecasts are transformed with the estimated parameters. This is minimum-CRPS estimation of a location-scale recalibration (Gneiting et al. 2005) applied to simulated paths: ranks within each cell are kept, so paths stay paths, and derived quantities such as life expectancy can be computed from the calibrated draws.

The wrapper works with any specification, including ensemble(), bootstrapped() and joint models. For reconciled() models the bottom strata are calibrated and the aggregates recomputed from them, so the draws stay coherent. With by, separate parameters are estimated for groups of strata (for example by = "sex"); strata outside these groups (aggregates) use the pooled parameters. Groups with different factors scale the common variation of joint models (such as the common trend of li_lee()) differently, so it no longer cancels in contrasts between the groups, and intervals of gaps between them widen; use pooled parameters when contrasts between the groups are the target.

Calibration needs years more training years than the base model. A spread factor above 1 means that the base model was too narrow in the window; it widens future intervals in proportion. The parameters are estimated from few overlapping forecasts (with the defaults, 5 origins and 30 forecast years, horizons 1 to 10), so they carry their own uncertainty, and they cannot anticipate changes after the window. Compare calibrated and uncalibrated models in an outer backtest.

In backtests on England & Wales men (HMD via StMoMo, origins 1996-2001, h = 10), calibration raised the 95% coverage of lee_carter() from 0.75 to 0.88 and lowered its CRPS by 4% (0.0687 to 0.0657); bias = TRUE gave the same. On the ONS deprivation data (6-year window), the coverage of Lee-Carter and Li-Lee rose with target = "interval" (0.83 to 0.90 and 0.84 to 0.89) at unchanged CRPS, and bias = TRUE made the CRPS worse (0.069 to 0.082). An equal-weight ensemble() of Lee-Carter and rwd() was already calibrated; calibration then narrowed it (95% coverage 0.93 to 0.85 on ONS, 0.95 to 0.90 on England & Wales) at the same CRPS (see the vignette "Forecasting mortality by deprivation quintile").

target = "crps" (default) balances calibration and sharpness; target = "interval" minimises the interval score of the central level interval (Gneiting and Raftery 2007), whose optimum is the correct coverage of that interval.

References

Gneiting T, Raftery AE, Westveld AH, Goldman T (2005). Calibrated probabilistic forecasting using ensemble model output statistics and minimum CRPS estimation. Monthly Weather Review 133(5): 1098-1118. doi:10.1175/MWR2904.1

Gneiting T, Raftery AE (2007). Strictly proper scoring rules, prediction, and estimation. Journal of the American Statistical Association 102(477): 359-378. doi:10.1198/016214506000001437

Examples

x <- mt_example(deaths = "single", years = 1990:2019)
fit <- mt_fit(calibrated(lee_carter(), years = 8, n_origins = 3, n_draws = 50), x)
fit$calibration
#>     group scale_h1      slope drift cells crps_before crps_after cov80_before
#>    <char>    <num>      <num> <num> <int>       <num>      <num>        <num>
#> 1:    all 1.244915 -0.9998819     0  2414  0.03398005 0.03389239    0.7692626
#>    cov80_after cov95_before cov95_after
#>          <num>        <num>       <num>
#> 1:   0.7228666    0.9092792   0.8719967
fc <- mt_forecast(fit, h = 5, n_draws = 100, seed = 1)
